title: Twelve digits of √2 in four steps
hook: Average a guess with 2 ÷ guess, again and again. How fast do the right digits pile up?

knows: decimals in a computer are approximations (pennies-dont-add-up)
doesNotKnow: that averaging a guess with 2/guess doubles the correct digits each step

misconception: Each guess gains about one more correct digit, so 12 digits needs about a dozen steps.
objective: The learner can explain that g -> (g + 2/g) / 2 from g = 1 gives 1, 1, 3, 6, 12 correct digits of √2, so 12 digits take four updates, because g and 2/g sit on opposite sides of √2 and the new error is about the old error squared.

claims.text: Your guesses had 1, 3, 6, then 12 correct digits: 12 after four updates, not twelve.
claims.source: Demo.tsx G and correctDigits(); builder's node script (2026-10-14), double precision: g = 1, 1.5, 1.4166666666666665, 1.4142156862745097, 1.4142135623746899; errors 0.41, 0.086, 0.0025, 2.1e-6, 1.6e-12. Digits counted by comparing the 17-significant-digit string of g with the true decimal expansion of √2 (1.41421356237309504880168872420969807856967187, OEIS A002193; cross-checked with a BigInt Newton iteration to 46 digits), not with Math.SQRT2. Matches the brief and spec. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Own node (fc21/newton.mjs) with the 45-digit sqrt(2) string, itself checked by a BigInt Newton root: digits 1, 1, 3, 6, 12, 15, 15 for g0..g6. Note for builder (not blocking): the reveal quotes updates 1-4 as '1, 3, 6, then 12', while this claim text includes g0 ('1, 1, 3, 6, then 12'); both are true, consider matching the claim text to the reveal. · Builder 2026-10-14 (W-198): reworded per pass 21; awaiting re-check. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Own run, sqrt(2) reference from my own BigInt Newton root: digits 1, 1, 3, 6, 12, 15, 15 for g0-g6; the reveal prints DIGITS[1..4] = 1, 3, 6, 12, matching the claim text.

claims.text: When g is too big, 2 ÷ g is too small by about the same amount, so their average lands much nearer √2.
claims.source: If g > √2 then 2/g < 2/√2 = √2. Writing g = √2 + e, 2/g = √2 - e + e²/√2 - ..., so 2/g is below √2 by about e, and the average is √2 + e²/(2√2) + O(e³). Shown on the stage's magnifier with exact decimal positions. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Own check: g = 1.5 is 0.0858 high, 2/g = 1.3333 is 0.0809 low; the expansion 2/(√2 + e) = √2 - e + e²/√2 - ... holds.

claims.text: The new error is about the old error squared (divided by 2.8), so the correct digits roughly double each update.
claims.source: From c2: e_new = e² / (2g) exactly (since (g + 2/g)/2 - √2 = (g - √2)² / (2g)), and 2g ≈ 2√2 ≈ 2.83 near the root. Squaring an error of 10^-k gives about 10^-2k, so correct digits double (quadratic convergence of Newton's method; e.g. Burden and Faires, Numerical Analysis, ch. 2, Newton's method). Check of the numbers: (2.1e-6)² / 2.83 = 1.6e-12. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Identity (g + 2/g)/2 - √2 = (g - √2)²/(2g) checked numerically: predicted next errors 8.58e-2, 2.45e-3, 2.12e-6, 1.59e-12 equal the actual ones.

claims.text: The fifth update reached 15 digits, the limit of the computer's numbers, and the sixth changed nothing.
claims.source: Builder's node script (2026-10-14): update 5 gives 1.4142135623730949 (15 correct significant digits against the true expansion; error 1.3e-16), and update 6 returns the identical double. A JavaScript number is an IEEE 754 double with a 53-bit significand, about 15.95 decimal digits, and the spacing of doubles near 1.414 is 2^-52 ≈ 2.2e-16: g5 and the computed 2/g5 (1.4142135623730951) are neighbouring doubles either side of √2, and their average rounds back to g5. Shown only if the learner ran to the end. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Own run: g5 = 1.4142135623730949, 15 digits, error -1.25e-16 (< 2^-52 ≈ 2.2e-16 spacing); g6 === g5. Caveat recorded: the nearest double to √2 (Math.SQRT2 = 1.4142135623730951) scores 16 by the lesson's own count, and is not itself a fixed point; '15 digits, the limit' is read as the usual ~15 reliable digits of a double (DBL_DIG = 15). Acceptable; builder may prefer 'about the limit'.

claims.text: This is Newton's method for g² = 2, the rule known as the Babylonian (or Heron's) method.
claims.source: Newton's update for f(g) = g² - 2 is g - f(g)/f'(g) = g - (g² - 2)/(2g) = (g + 2/g)/2, the same as averaging g and 2/g (derivation). The averaging rule is conventionally named the Babylonian (or Heron's) method; Heron of Alexandria describes it in Metrica (1st century AD; not opened by the builder). The sentence asserts only the name, not that any Babylonian tablet used this rule. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: c5 DISPUTED (historical half unchecked: YBC 7289 method not recorded); Fowler & Robson 1998 reconstruct a geometric method. · Builder 2026-10-14 (W-198): reworded per pass 21; awaiting re-check. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: HELD, not verified. Newton half re-derived: g - (g^2 - 2)/(2g) = (g + 2/g)/2. The naming half ('known as the Babylonian (or Heron's) method') is a historical-naming fact that only an outside source can establish, and every host was unreachable (wikipedia, mathpages, arxiv: DNS failure); only search-result summaries agree. Per the pass-23 rule I do not verify on a source I cannot open. To clear: a human opens any reference (e.g. Wikipedia 'Methods of computing square roots') or the builder drops the naming clause.

recall.question: A Newton update for a square root has a guess right to 5 digits. About how many correct digits does the next update give?
recall.why: Near the root the new error is about the old error squared, so an error near 10^-5 becomes about 10^-10: the correct digits roughly double, to about 10.
